title: The Inverse of a Matrix is a Polynomial in the Matrix
description: A constructive corollary of Cayley–Hamilton: for an invertible matrix A over a field, A⁻¹ = (aeval A) r for an explicit polynomial r = C(−c₀)⁻¹·divX(charpoly A) of degree < n, where c₀ = (charpoly A).coeff 0 = ±det A. Hence the inverse lies in the subalgebra K[A] generated by A.

overview.historicalContext: The Cayley–Hamilton theorem states that every square matrix satisfies its own characteristic polynomial. One of its most useful consequences is computational: when A is invertible, the relation p(A) = 0 can be rearranged to express A⁻¹ as a polynomial in A of degree less than n. This avoids the adjugate/cofactor formula and shows, structurally, that the inverse already lives inside the commutative subalgebra K[A] generated by A — a fact that underlies algorithms for matrix inversion via the characteristic polynomial (e.g. the Faddeev–LeVerrier method) and the theory of the rational canonical form.
overview.problemStatement: Prove that the inverse of an invertible matrix A over a field is the evaluation at A of an explicit polynomial of degree < n, and deduce that A⁻¹ lies in the subalgebra generated by A.
overview.text: From Cayley–Hamilton p(A)=0, split p = divX(p)·X + C c₀ with c₀ = ±det A ≠ 0; then (divX p)(A)·A = −c₀•1, so A⁻¹ = (−c₀)⁻¹·(divX p)(A) = (aeval A) r with deg r < n.
overview.proofStrategy: Write p = charpoly A. Evaluating the algebraic identity divX(p)·X + C(p.coeff 0) = p at A turns Cayley–Hamilton into (divX p)(A)·A + c₀•1 = 0. The identity det A = (−1)^n · c₀ shows det A ≠ 0 ⟹ c₀ ≠ 0, so −c₀ is a unit; dividing yields a left inverse ((−c₀)⁻¹•(divX p)(A))·A = 1 that equals the polynomial (aeval A) (C(−c₀)⁻¹·divX p). Matrix.inv_eq_left_inv promotes the left inverse to A⁻¹, and mul_eq_one_comm gives the right-inverse companion. The degree bound combines natDegree_C_mul_le with degree_divX_lt and charpoly_natDegree_eq_dim; membership in K[A] follows from adjoin_singleton_eq_range_aeval.
keyInsights: Cayley–Hamilton in additive form: peeling off the constant term of charpoly turns p(A)=0 into a relation that isolates A·(polynomial in A) = scalar
The constant term c₀ = (charpoly A).coeff 0 equals ±det A, so invertibility is exactly the condition that makes c₀ a unit
Dividing by the unit −c₀ produces an explicit polynomial whose evaluation is the inverse — no adjugate needed
Because the inverse is a polynomial in A, it automatically commutes with A and lies in the commutative subalgebra K[A]
The degree bound deg r < n is forced by divX dropping the degree of the monic degree-n characteristic polynomial

sections.title: Documentation and Setup
sections.summary: Header deriving A⁻¹ as a polynomial in A from Cayley–Hamilton. Sets up a field K and matrices over a finite index type n, and defines the inverse polynomial invPoly A.
sections.mathContext: The setup `{n : Type*} [DecidableEq n] [Fintype n]`, `{K : Type*} [Field K]` works for any finite square matrix over a field; invertibility enters as the hypothesis det A ≠ 0.

sections.title: The Constant Term is a Unit
sections.summary: charpoly_coeff_zero_ne_zero: det A ≠ 0 implies (charpoly A).coeff 0 ≠ 0, using det = (−1)^n · coeff 0.
sections.mathContext: The constant term of the characteristic polynomial is ±det A, so invertibility is precisely what makes it a nonzero scalar that we may invert.

sections.title: Cayley–Hamilton in Additive Form
sections.summary: aeval_divX_mul_self: evaluating divX(charpoly)·X + C c₀ = charpoly at A gives (divX p)(A)·A + c₀•1 = 0.
sections.mathContext: Splitting off the constant term lets Cayley–Hamilton be read as a relation of the form (something)·A = scalar, the key to isolating the inverse.

sections.title: The Inverse as a Polynomial
sections.summary: aeval_invPoly_mul_self and inv_eq_aeval_invPoly: (aeval A)(invPoly A) is a left inverse of A, hence equals A⁻¹.
sections.mathContext: Dividing the additive Cayley–Hamilton relation by the unit −c₀ produces a left inverse that is visibly a polynomial in A; Matrix.inv_eq_left_inv identifies it with the nonsingular inverse.

sections.title: Degree Bound, Subalgebra Membership, and Packaging
sections.summary: invPoly_natDegree_lt (deg < n), inv_mem_adjoin (A⁻¹ ∈ K[A]), self_mul_aeval_invPoly (right inverse), exists_inv_eq_aeval (packaged existence).
sections.mathContext: The inverse polynomial has degree below n and lives in the subalgebra generated by A, so A⁻¹ commutes with A and is a genuine polynomial expression in it.

conclusion.summary: From Cayley–Hamilton, the inverse of any invertible matrix over a field is the evaluation at A of an explicit polynomial of degree < n, and therefore lies in the subalgebra K[A]. All 8 theorems and 1 definition are fully verified with 0 sorries and 0 axioms.
conclusion.implications: This is the structural basis for characteristic-polynomial-based inversion (Faddeev–LeVerrier) and shows A⁻¹ ∈ K[A], so the inverse commutes with A and with everything that commutes with A.
openQuestions: Extract the Faddeev–LeVerrier recurrence for the coefficients of invPoly from the Newton identities, giving an explicit algorithm for the inverse polynomial.
